convergence: Both responses propose a phased framework that rejects both a total moratorium and unregulated operation. Both identify the same four core problem areas: liability/insurance, safety standards, economic transition for taxi drivers, and geographic equity in testing. Both propose similar concrete mechanisms: permit-conditioned strict liability for the AV company, a surety bond or self-insurance requirement, a fleet cap in the city center, a per-ride surcharge feeding into a driver transition fund, proportional distribution of testing miles across districts, and third-party validation of sensor reliability for vulnerable road users. Both frame their approach as balancing competing demands rather than choosing one side entirely.

divergences.location: Safety Standards section — the core operational model during the transition period
divergences.response_a: Proposes a geographic suspension: AVs continue operating city-wide, but are excluded from high-pedestrian zones for 60 days while the company submits simulation and closed-course testing data proving wheelchair-user detection capability.
divergences.response_b: Proposes a capability suspension: AVs continue operating everywhere, but only with trained human safety drivers behind the wheel (Tier 1), with a pathway to uncrewed operation (Tier 2) once 99.99% sensor reliability is proven.
divergences.nature: Response A restricts where AVs can operate; Response B restricts how they operate. Response A allows uncrewed autonomous driving in lower-pedestrian areas immediately; Response B suspends all uncrewed operation city-wide until a specific reliability threshold is met.
divergences.specificity: Response A leaves open what happens after 60 days and does not specify a numerical reliability target. Response B names a specific threshold (99.99%) and creates two explicit tiers with clear transition conditions, but does not specify how long Tier 1 will last or what happens if the threshold is not met.

divergences.location: Safety Standards section — the form and venue of validation testing
divergences.response_a: Requires "independent, third-party audited data" from "closed-course testing and simulations" to prove sensor recognition of wheelchair users.
divergences.response_b: Requires validation "conducted in closed-course municipal testing centers and verified by a third-party auditor," and adds a separate requirement for "data sharing" on disengagements and near-misses with the City Transport Authority.
divergences.nature: Response A specifies the form of evidence (audited data from testing and simulation); Response B specifies the venue (municipal testing centers) and adds an ongoing data-sharing obligation separate from the validation gateway. Response B creates a continuous monitoring mechanism; Response A focuses on a one-time proof point.
divergences.specificity: Response A does not specify where testing occurs or what happens to data after validation. Response B names the venue explicitly and creates an ongoing reporting requirement to the Transport Authority, but does not specify what the city will do with the shared data or how it will be used to track progress.

divergences.location: Economic Stability section — the mechanism for protecting taxi drivers
divergences.response_a: Proposes a fleet cap and per-ride surcharge, with revenue going to a "Driver Transition & Transit Fund" for "retraining programs, benefits, or subsidized operational costs."
divergences.response_b: Proposes a fleet cap with year-over-year increases tied to safety milestones, a per-ride surcharge with a specific range ($0.50–$1.00), and a "Mobility Transition Fund" that is "overseen by the city and the union." Additionally proposes geofenced speed limits (20 mph) in the city center.
divergences.nature: Response A describes the fund's purpose in general terms; Response B specifies the surcharge amount, adds governance structure (joint city-union oversight), and introduces an additional safety mechanism (geofenced speed limits) not present in Response A.
divergences.specificity: Response A leaves the surcharge amount unspecified and does not address how the fund will be governed or who decides how money is allocated. Response B provides a price range and names joint governance but does not specify what "safety milestones" trigger the year-over-year cap increases or how they are measured.

divergences.location: Equity section — the form of intervention in low-income neighborhoods
divergences.response_a: Proposes two interventions: (1) proportional distribution of testing miles across districts, and (2) temporary restriction of AVs from roads with "critically degraded infrastructure" until the city repairs them, which "incentivizes the city to upgrade infrastructure in low-income areas."
divergences.response_b: Proposes two interventions: (1) proportional distribution of testing miles with routing algorithm audits to ensure low-income neighborhoods do not exceed their demographic share, and (2) a "Community Benefit Mandate" requiring a percentage of the AV fleet to serve transit deserts at subsidized rates.
divergences.nature: Response A uses infrastructure repair as a lever to prevent testing in degraded areas and incentivize city investment; Response B uses fleet allocation and subsidized service as a lever to direct AV resources toward underserved communities. Response A focuses on preventing harm; Response B focuses on creating benefit.
divergences.specificity: Response A does not specify what percentage of infrastructure degradation triggers the restriction or how the city will prioritize repairs. Response B does not specify what percentage of the fleet must serve transit deserts or what "subsidized rates" means in practice.

divergences.location: Overall structure and presentation of the framework
divergences.response_a: Organizes the framework into four pillars, then adds a separate section titled "How This Balances Competing Demands" that explicitly maps each pillar back to the original tensions (safety vs. innovation, economic tension, equity, innovation).
divergences.response_b: Organizes the framework into four sections, then adds a "Summary of the Compromise" that lists what each stakeholder group receives (AV company, pedestrians, taxi union, low-income communities).
divergences.nature: Response A's closing section explains how the framework resolves the underlying conflicts; Response B's closing section enumerates the benefits to each stakeholder. Response A emphasizes the problem-solving logic; Response B emphasizes the distribution of outcomes.
divergences.specificity: Response A's closing section is more abstract, referring back to the original problem tensions without quantifying or detailing outcomes. Response B's closing section is more concrete, listing specific protections for each group, but does not explain how the framework resolves the tensions between them.

divergences.location: Treatment of the 40% safety improvement statistic
divergences.response_a: Uses the 40% improvement as a reason to reject a moratorium ("forfeit the proven 40% overall safety improvement") and as justification for allowing continued operation while adding targeted restrictions.
divergences.response_b: Uses the 40% improvement as a reason to reject the taxi union's total ban ("incompatible with the city's safety goals given AVs have 40% fewer accidents overall") but does not emphasize it as a reason to preserve uncrewed operation.
divergences.nature: Both responses invoke the statistic to reject a moratorium, but Response A treats it as a positive outcome to preserve through continued operation, while Response B treats it as a fact that makes a ban unjustifiable, without necessarily implying that the current operational model should continue unchanged.
divergences.specificity: Response A makes the 40% improvement central to the case for allowing AVs to remain; Response B mentions it as context for why a ban is unreasonable but does not build the safety case around preserving this specific outcome.
